# Lead-Time Compression Plan: From 14 Weeks to Competitive Speed Without Touching the Quality Gates

## 1. The Core Reframe: Compress Waiting, Not Work

The last compression attempt failed because it almost certainly compressed the wrong thing — rushing assembly, squeezing inspections, accepting marginal parts, running fatigued overtime. That trades lead time for warranty claims, and the organization paid for it for two years.

The decisive insight of manufacturing lead-time analysis: **in most industrial equipment operations, actual value-added touch time is 5–15% of total lead time.** The other 85–95% is queue, waiting, batching, handoffs, inspection backlogs, procurement lag, and schedule padding. A 14-week quote on a product with perhaps 10–15 days of real work is not a speed problem — it's a flow problem.

This reframe matters politically as much as technically: **nobody has to work faster, and no inspection gets shortened.** The plan removes the idle time *between* the work. That is the only framing that gets Quality to the table without a veto and prevents a repeat of the warranty disaster.

---

## 2. Diagnose Before Cutting: Map Where the 14 Weeks Actually Go

Resist all pressure to act before the facts exist. In weeks 1–8, build a **lead-time waterfall** by time-stamping 3–5 representative recent orders end-to-end:

| Stage | Typical Finding | Likely Hidden Delay |
|---|---|---|
| Order entry → engineering release | 1–3 weeks | Orders queue for engineering; every order treated as custom |
| Procurement of long-lead items | 4–8 weeks | Suppliers engaged only *after* order release; castings, drives, motors, electronics stack serially into the critical path |
| Fabrication / machining | 2–3 weeks elapsed | Days of queue for hours of cutting; large batches; bottleneck machine starved then flooded |
| In-process certified inspections | Adds days per gate | Parts wait for a small pool of certified inspectors and limited test equipment — the inspection takes hours, the queue takes days |
| Assembly | 1–2 weeks | Kit shortages, rework loops from defects found late |
| Final certified test + third-party witness | 1–2 weeks | Witness scheduling lead time; test cell is a hidden bottleneck |
| Certification documentation package | 3–7 days | Dossier compiled *after* the build instead of during it |
| Crating / shipping | 2–5 days | — |
| Embedded padding | 15–25% of quote | Each function pads because it doesn't trust the others |

Also complete in this phase:
- **Identify the true constraint** (usually one machine, the test cell, or the inspection lab) — everything else must subordinate to it.
- **Blameless after-action review of the previous failure:** which specific shortcuts caused which warranty claims? Codify the answers as explicit design constraints ("we will never again reduce X, skip Y, or accept Z under schedule pressure"). This converts scar tissue into specification.
- **Validate the commercial case:** if one in three losses is delivery-driven, recovering even a fraction of those deals likely dwarfs the cost of added inspection capacity and strategic inventory. Quantify it — this funds the program.

---

## 3. The Biggest Strategic Lever: Move the Decoupling Point

A 14-week quote usually means the company builds everything from scratch after the order arrives. The single most powerful change is restructuring *what waits for the customer*:

- **Modularize the product** into pre-engineered standard modules with defined option interfaces, so most orders become *configurations*, not engineering projects. Engineering leaves the critical path for 70–80% of orders.
- **Pre-build standard subassemblies and stock long-lead components** against forecast. Quoted lead time then = final assembly + test + documentation + ship — which can be 6–8 weeks even if total build time is longer.
- **Differentiate the quote by configuration:** standard models at 6 weeks, configured orders at 8, full custom at 10–12. Sales stops quoting one padded number for everything and gains a competitive menu. A premium expedite lane (see §6) captures the most delivery-sensitive deals at margin.

This is how a manufacturer *substantially* cuts quoted lead time without anyone working faster: the customer simply arrives after the slow parts are already done.

---

## 4. Process Changes

- **Cut batch sizes.** Large batches exist to "save setups," but they multiply queue time everywhere (Little's Law: at constant throughput, lead time scales with WIP). Halving batch sizes roughly halves queue time.
- **SMED setup reduction** on the constraint and high-changeover machines, so small batches become economical instead of painful.
- **Flow cells for product families** — group machines by product routing, not by department, to eliminate handoff queues.
- **Standard work** at assembly and test to stabilize cycle times; unstable cycle times are why everyone pads.
- **Fix first-pass yield as a lead-time program, not just a quality program.** Rework discovered at final test is the hidden schedule killer — it consumes bottleneck capacity twice and makes dates unpredictable. Run a Pareto on the top five defect modes, root-cause them, and mistake-proof (poka-yoke) the sources.

---

## 5. Inventory Changes

- **Strategic buffers of long-lead purchased items** (castings, motors, drives, specialty alloys, electronics) sized from forecast and consumption variability — this is deliberate, surgically placed inventory, not blanket stockpiling.
- **Subassembly supermarkets** holding standard modules at the decoupling point.
- **Consignment / vendor-managed inventory** for high-usage, low-cost hardware so shortages never stall assembly.
- **Buffer placement per Theory of Constraints:** a controlled buffer *before* the constraint and *before* the certified final test cell, so the two resources that govern lead time are never starved.
- **Aggressively reduce WIP everywhere else.** The trade is explicit: less inventory scattered randomly across the floor, more inventory placed deliberately where it buys lead time.

---

## 6. Scheduling Changes

- **Finite-capacity scheduling** built around the constraint (drum-buffer-rope): the constraint sets the drumbeat, everything else synchronizes to it, and a time buffer protects delivery promises.
- **Capable-to-promise quoting:** Sales quotes from live capacity slots in the scheduling system, not from a fixed 14-week blanket number. Quotes become differentiated, credible, and fast — quote turnaround itself is often a hidden deal-loser.
- **Level the load.** Kill the end-of-quarter surge that wrecks flow and forces padding; smooth release of orders to the floor.
- **One controlled expedite lane**, capped at a small percentage of capacity with strict triage rules. Uncontrolled expediting is how plants destroy themselves: every expedite becomes a delay for ten other orders, which then become expedites.
- **Kill the padding** once flow stabilizes — padding is a symptom of distrust, and it inflates quoted lead time directly. Replace negotiated buffers with measured ones.

---

## 7. Supplier Changes

- **Share rolling forecasts and issue blanket POs with releases**, so supplier capacity is reserved before the order arrives rather than quoted after it.
- **Supplier lead-time reduction projects** with the top five long-lead suppliers — their queues have the same structure as yours.
- **Certified supplier program enabling dock-to-line:** suppliers who demonstrate sustained quality (audited, PPM-tracked) skip the incoming inspection queue, with periodic verification. This removes days from every order without weakening a single certified gate — it relocates the assurance upstream to the source.
- **Dual-source or qualify alternates** for the longest-lead, highest-risk items; evaluate regional sourcing where freight time is material.
- **Early supplier involvement** on new configurations so manufacturability and lead time are designed in, not discovered.

---

## 8. Protecting the Quality Gates — Explicitly and Visibly

This section is the price of admission for Quality's support, and it must be **written, signed, and non-negotiable**:

1. **The Quality Non-Negotiables Charter:** certified inspection gates, acceptance criteria, sample sizes, and test durations are fixed. No lead-time initiative may alter a certified gate without the Quality Director's sign-off and, where applicable, customer or certifying-body approval. Quality holds a veto over gate changes — but not over flow changes.
2. **Attack the inspection *queue*, never the inspection.** Add certified inspector capacity, test equipment, and shift coverage so inspection availability matches production rhythm. If production runs two shifts and the lab runs one, the lab is the schedule.
3. **Move verification upstream:** first-article checks, in-process probing, operator self-verification with mistake-proofing, and statistical process control — so certified gates become fast *confirmations* of a capable process rather than *discovery* points that trigger rework.
4. **Pre-book third-party witness slots** on a rolling basis against the schedule, and negotiate remote/virtual witnessing where the certifying body permits. Witness availability should never be an unplanned critical-path item.
5. **Build the certification dossier in parallel with the product** via digital quality records, not as a paper chase after final test.
6. **Pre-agreed containment triggers:** if first-pass yield at any gate drops below threshold, the plan automatically slows flow and escalates — rather than shipping risk. This is the structural answer to "last time we went fast, customers paid for it."

Note the commercial upside: certified quality, reliably fast, is a *stronger* competitive position than the competitor's 6 weeks with weaker credentials. Don't race them on their terms; beat them on speed-plus-proof.

---

## 9. Aligning Production, Quality, and Sales

The feud persists because each function is measured so that it wins by making the others lose. Dismantle that deliberately:

- **One set of facts.** All three functions walk the value stream mapping exercise *together* and co-sign the lead-time waterfall. When everyone sees that 85% of the time is queue — belonging to no single department — the blame conversation runs out of fuel. This is the single most important alignment move.
- **One scorecard.** A shared dashboard reviewed together weekly: quoted vs. actual lead time, on-time delivery, first-pass yield per gate, warranty rate. **Rule: speed metrics are never reviewed without quality metrics beside them.** No function can optimize at another's expense because no function is scored alone.
- **Aligned incentives:** a meaningful portion of variable compensation for leaders in all three functions tied to the *same* combined metric — on-time-in-full at quoted lead time, at or above quality thresholds. Sales commission must not reward booking orders with dates the plant can't meet.
- **Quoting discipline:** Sales quotes only from the capable-to-promise system; exceptions go to a deal desk with Production and Quality sign-off. No more heroic promises that become the plant's emergency.
- **S&OP cadence:** monthly, Sales brings pipeline and forecast; Production commits capacity and the pre-positioning plan; Quality confirms gate capacity and witness scheduling. No side deals.
- **Governance:** an executive-sponsored, cross-functional lead-time team with real authority, a weekly tiered review, and a visual war-room board. The sponsor (COO/GM) owns tie-breaking.
- **Sequence trust-building:** start with quick wins that cost little and risk nothing — pre-booked witness slots, parallel documentation, quote-from-capacity for one product line. Early visible success buys permission for the harder structural changes.

---

## 10. Measure What Matters

| Category | Metrics |
|---|---|
| **Speed** | Quoted vs. actual lead time; order-to-delivery days; touch-time ratio (% of lead time that's value-added); quote turnaround time |
| **Reliability** | On-time delivery to quoted date; schedule adherence; expedite share of orders |
| **Quality (always paired with speed)** | First-pass yield per gate; gate cycle time (queue + inspection); escapes; warranty claim rate and cost |
| **Flow** | WIP levels; batch sizes; setup times; constraint utilization; test-cell and inspection-lab queue days |
| **Suppliers** | Supplier lead time and on-time delivery; incoming PPM; % of spend dock-to-line |
| **Commercial** | Win rate on delivery-sensitive deals; margin on expedite lane; lost-deal reasons (validated, not self-reported) |

**Beware vanity metrics:** machine utilization is the enemy here — running equipment to look busy builds WIP and *lengthens* lead time. Measure flow, not busyness.

---

## 11. Implementation Roadmap

| Phase | Timeframe | Actions | Quoted Lead-Time Target |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1. Diagnose & charter** | Weeks 1–8 | Lead-time waterfall; constraint ID; blameless review of past failure; Quality Non-Negotiables Charter signed; baseline metrics; quick wins (witness pre-booking, parallel documentation) | 14 weeks (unchanged — promise nothing yet) |
| **2. Stabilize & quick compression** | Months 2–6 | Strategic inventory of top long-lead items; batch-size reduction + SMED on constraint; added inspection capacity; supplier forecast sharing; capable-to-promise quoting for standard line | **10 weeks** |
| **3. Flow & model change** | Months 6–12 | Modularization / configure-to-order; subassembly supermarkets; flow cells; dock-to-line suppliers; differentiated quoting (6 / 8 / 10–12) with expedite lane | **6–8 weeks standard** |
| **4. Sustain & adapt** | Ongoing | S&OP rhythm; annual value-stream refresh; continuous FPY improvement; quarterly supplier reviews; automatic containment triggers | Hold and improve |

---

## 12. Key Pitfalls to Avoid

- **Compressing work instead of waiting** — the exact mistake of last time. If anyone proposes shortening a test, reducing a sample, or "trusting the supplier this once" to hit a date, the charter exists to stop it.
- **Expediting everything.** A plant where every order is hot has no schedule at all.
- **Optimizing utilization over flow.** Busy machines and long lead times are the same decision.
- **Sales quoting around the system.** One heroic side-promise re-poisons trust faster than ten kept dates rebuild it.
- **Big-bang rollout.** Pilot on one product family, prove the model, then scale.
- **Reviewing speed and quality in separate meetings.** Separation is how the old failure mode sneaks back in.
- **Starving the constraint or the test cell** while improving everything else — lead time is set at the bottleneck, full stop.

---

**Bottom line:** The 14-week quote is not fourteen weeks of work — it is roughly two weeks of work wrapped in twelve weeks of waiting, batching, procurement lag, inspection queues, and defensive padding. Cut the waiting and the quote falls to 6–8 weeks without a single certified gate being touched: move the decoupling point so slow work finishes before the customer arrives, shrink batches and protect the bottleneck so flow replaces queue, add inspection *capacity* instead of inspection *pressure*, and pull supplier lead times out of the critical path. Bind Production, Quality, and Sales to one set of facts, one scorecard, and one signed charter that makes the quality gates untouchable — so this time, speed and quality stop being rivals and become the same competitive weapon: the fastest *credible* promise in the market, kept every time.
